projects.tagline: A Lean proof that $p_{n+1} - p_n \leq 246$ for infinitely many $n$.
projects.summary: Formalizes Maynard's multidimensional sieve and the part of Polymath8b that brings the bound to $246$, on top of Mathlib and Kontorovich and Tao's PrimeNumberTheoremAnd. The Lean code is released as PrimeGapsLib.

projects.title: The Classification of Finite Simple Groups, Formalized in Lean

ai.label: AI-assisted
ai.note: The Lean proofs were produced by swarms of AxiomProver agents; the mathematical obstructions they ran into were handled by hand.

projects.tagline: A Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, following the first-generation proof.
projects.summary: Every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of the 26 sporadic groups. The original proof runs to some 15,000 journal pages written over several decades; the formalization is about 43 million lines of Lean, produced over 24 days.
description: Formalizing the first-generation argument turned up counterexamples to a closure assertion used in a published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem. That and the other departures from the literature are recorded in the errata.

outputs.scope: The counterexamples, and an alternative argument for the simple-group case using Solomon's theory of maximal 2-components.

projects.title: The Stacks Project, Formalized in Lean
projects.role: Project lead; mathematical and engineering contributor

ai.label: AI-assisted
ai.note: The Lean proofs were produced by AxiomProver agents, then reviewed and brought up to Mathlib standards.

projects.tagline: A Lean formalization of the Stacks Project, the open-source reference work on algebraic geometry.
projects.summary: The Stacks Project is the standard open-source reference on algebraic geometry, a collaboratively written work of some 7,500 pages covering commutative algebra, schemes, cohomology and the theory of algebraic stacks, with every definition, lemma, proposition and theorem carrying a stable four-character tag. The formalization runs to 663,090 Lean declarations across about 15.75 million lines, built on Mathlib, with Lean's kernel checking every completed proof and each tag linked to its Lean code and its dependencies.
description: The emphasis throughout is on code quality: definitions and statements are written to Mathlib standards and at the generality their consumers need, so that the library is something to build on and to upstream from, rather than a pile of individually verified theorems.

projects.title: The Weil Conjectures, Formalized in Lean

ai.label: AI-assisted
ai.note: The Lean proofs were produced by AxiomProver agents, and Lean's kernel checks every one of them.

projects.tagline: The Weil conjectures proved in Lean on top of the Stacks Project formalization, at a seventieth of its size.
projects.summary: Deligne's theorem is about as deep as algebraic geometry gets, and the étale cohomology it runs on is exactly what the Stacks Project in Lean supplies. All four conjectures — rationality, the functional equation, the Riemann hypothesis and the Betti-number statement — are proved in 213,000 lines of new Lean, following Freitag and Kiehl.
description: The point is reuse. The library imports 730 modules of the Stacks formalization against 557 of Mathlib, more than half its files depend on Stacks directly, and it cites 283 Stacks tags; Deligne's theorem itself falls out of the Stacks weight bound at Tag 03VH rather than being proved again.
Quality carries over with the code. The library takes the Stacks conventions — the same étale site, the same $\ell$-adic sheaves — pins the same Mathlib commit, and is written to the same standard.

projects.title: Introduction to Cluster Algebras, Formalized in Lean

ai.label: AI-assisted
ai.note: The blueprint was written by hand; AxiomProver agents formalized it entry by entry, and Lean's kernel checks every proof.

projects.tagline: Chapters 1–7 of Fomin, Williams and Zelevinsky's Introduction to Cluster Algebras, formalized in Lean.
projects.summary: A cluster algebra is a commutative ring generated by cluster variables, grouped into clusters and produced from an initial seed by mutation; since Fomin and Zelevinsky introduced them in 2002 they have turned up in total positivity, representation theory, Teichmüller theory, Poisson geometry and the combinatorics of the Grassmannian. The library follows the book statement by statement, formalizing 1,348 of its 1,429 blueprint entries in some 330,000 lines of Lean on top of Mathlib, as far as the Laurent phenomenon, the finite type classification, Scott's theorem that the Plücker ring of a Grassmannian is a cluster algebra, and the fundamental theorem of reduced plabic graphs.
description: What the library assumes is visible in its statements. Results the book takes from elsewhere, the Cartan–Killing classification among them, are Lean propositions carried as explicit hypotheses by every theorem that uses them, so the library declares no axioms of its own; six of the exercises the book leaves to the reader are proved outright.

The finite type classification is proved one Cartan–Killing type at a time, and for $E_8$ the 128 cluster variables and 25,080 clusters are certified by a computation Lean's kernel checks. Eleven headline theorems are restated in a separate challenge file, and Lean's comparator checks against two independent kernels that the library proves exactly those statements.

ai.label: AI-assisted

projects.tagline: Faltings' theorem in Lean: a curve of genus at least two over a number field has only finitely many rational points.
projects.summary: The first complete machine-checked proof of the Mordell conjecture, following Bombieri's rendering of Vojta's proof. The Stacks Project formalization supplies the schemes, curves, Picard groups, cohomology and abelian varieties; heights on projective space, the Mordell–Weil theorem, the Jacobian and its theta divisor, the Néron–Tate pairing and Bombieri's estimates are new, about 124,000 lines of Lean.
description: Stacks carries the weight. The library imports 336 modules of the Stacks formalization against 26 of Mathlib, and 194 of its 432 files depend on Stacks directly — the arithmetic is what had to be built, not the algebraic geometry under it.

The statement is checked against someone else's. LeanEval's faltings problem defines places, adeles and the genus of a function field from Mathlib alone; that statement is proved verbatim, with its own definitions, and the library's genus is shown to agree with it. The theorem is also stated scheme-theoretically, for a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus at least two over a number field.
